newsitem.title: INDIA: FOCUS-India budget delights business, irks Left.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-India budget delights business, irks Left.

text.p: India's government proposed bold tax cuts on Friday in a budget plan that delighted business but irritated its communist partners.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram told parliament the government would slash corporate and personal taxes, and trim import duties in the 1997/98 fiscal year starting on April 1.

The proposed moves sent share prices soaring as investors anticipated a spurt in corporate profits. The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark index jumped 178.20 points, or 5.13 percent, to 3,652.99 in a special late-evening session.
"Both me and my markets are very happy," said Bombay Stock Exchange president Madan Gopal Damani.
Business leaders were enthused by a plan to reduce the tax on domestic corporations to 35 percent from 40 percent, and abolish a tax on income from dividends.

The budget, which must be approved by parliament, would allow foreign investors to take stakes of up to 30 percent in Indian companies, up from 24 percent, and cut personal income tax rates across the board.
"This is definitely a budget for industry," said R.S. Cheema, managing director of DLF Industries Ltd.
"It's far bolder than expected," said Harish Mariwala, managing director of Marico Industries Ltd.

Chidambaram's sympathy for the business community, which had lamented a slowdown in industrial growth and sluggish share prices, drew a lukewarm response from left-wing parties within Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 15-party minority coalition.
"There is not much to encourage agriculture in this budget," grumbled Agriculture Minister Chaturanan Mishra of the Communist Party of India (CPI).
CPI leaders said the cut in customs duties meant foreign firms might take over Indian companies. They also complained about a rise in postal rates.

But the government, with an eye on the Left, stopped short of raising oil prices to stem a runaway subsidy bill, and proposed only a modest opening up of the state-run insurance industry which has hundreds of thousands of workers.

Chidambaram said the fiscal deficit as a share of gross domestic prodcut (GDP) -- considered a barometer of the economy's overall health -- would drop to 5.0 percent in the 1996/97 financial year ending on March 31, from 5.5 percent.
He said the centre-left government which took office last June aimed to cut the fiscal deficit to 4.5 percent of GDP in the next financial year starting on April 1.
"We have maintained the fiscal discipline, and next year there will be even more discipline," Chidambaram said.

Offsetting tax cuts, the budget would extend the tax net, currently limited to only about 12 million of India's 936 million citizens, by imposing new levies on owners of cars and telephones, and raising excise taxes on cigarettes.
But the claims of fiscal discipline met with some scepticism. "Where is the government going to get the money?" said Amit Ghosh of HSBC Investment Bank.
"Inflation will increase," said Atal Bihari Vajpayee, leader of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The Congress party, which was trounced in polls last year and gives Deve Gowda crucial support, voiced subdued criticism.

Former finance minister Manmohan Singh said he was worried about inflation and overspending, but welcomed the overall thrust. "This is the endorsement of the policies followed by the Congress government," he said.
